# Spanish {#sec-spanish}

*Padrenuestro* — also called the *oración dominical*, the prayer of the Lord.
Spanish inherited the prayer through the Latin of the Vulgate, and the biblical
wording below is the point where the Catholic and Protestant traditions in
Spanish happen to agree almost word for word: it is common to Felipe Scío de
San Miguel's 1793 translation of the Vulgate and to the Reina-Valera.

## The text

::: {.prayer lang="es" speech="es-ES" #es-biblical}
| Padre nuestro, que estás en los cielos,
| santificado sea tu Nombre;
| venga a nosotros tu reino;
| hágase tu voluntad así en la tierra como en el cielo.
| El pan nuestro de cada día dánosle hoy;
| y perdónanos nuestras deudas
| como también nosotros perdonamos a nuestros deudores;
| y no nos dejes caer en la tentación,
| mas líbranos del mal.
:::

Reina-Valera renders the fifth line as *danos hoy nuestro pan cotidiano*.

## The liturgical variant

The form said aloud at Mass differs from the biblical text in one theologically
loaded place. Where the Greek has *ὀφειλήματα* and the Latin *debita* —
**debts** — the Spanish liturgy says **ofensas**, offences:

::: {.prayer lang="es" speech="es-ES" #es-liturgical .variant}
| Padre nuestro, que estás en el cielo,
| santificado sea tu Nombre;
| venga a nosotros tu reino;
| hágase tu voluntad en la tierra como en el cielo.
| Danos hoy nuestro pan de cada día;
| perdona nuestras ofensas,
| como también nosotros perdonamos a los que nos ofenden;
| no nos dejes caer en la tentación,
| y líbranos del mal.
| Amén.
:::

Spanish is not alone in this: Portuguese, Galician and French all made the same
substitution, while English, Italian and German kept the debt. The Spanish
Wikipedia article treats the swap as a real change of meaning rather than a
stylistic one — a debt is something owed and quantifiable, an offence is
something felt.

## Note on the doxology

Spanish Catholic practice does not attach *porque tuyo es el reino* to the end
of the prayer; at Mass it comes back after the priest's embolism. Protestant
usage generally does attach it.
